title: PostgreSQL Index Types: B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Partial, and Expression Indexes
description: PostgreSQL Index Types: B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Partial, and Expression Indexes. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Match PostgreSQL index families to operators and data shape.
Explain GIN, GiST, and BRIN trade-offs.
Use partial and expression indexes when predicates match.

mentalModel.text: An index is useful only when its operator class supports query operators. B-tree is the general default for equality, ranges, and ordering; GIN indexes component values; GiST provides generalized search structures; BRIN summarizes physical block ranges. Partial and expression indexes specialize which rows or expressions are indexed.

blocks.text: B-tree is the general-purpose PostgreSQL index for equality, inequalities, ranges, and compatible ordering. Hash supports equality but not ordered range traversal.

blocks.title: Key distinctions
rows: Structure used to locate candidate rows

blocks.text: GIN maps component keys to rows containing those keys. It can support array membership, JSONB containment, and text-search patterns when the operator class supports the operator.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX products_attrs_gin ON products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

steps.title: Identify query shape
steps.description: Write down predicates, joins, ordering, limit, and selected columns.

steps.title: Predict the mechanism
steps.description: Explain which pages, entries, or operators the database is likely to visit.

steps.title: Validate the plan
steps.description: Use actual rows and buffers to compare prediction with observed work.

blocks.text: GiST is a generalized search-tree framework with operator-class-specific behavior. BRIN stores summaries for heap block ranges and is compact when values correlate with physical row order, but summaries are lossy and require rechecks.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX events_created_brin ON events USING BRIN (created_at);

blocks.problem: A query is slower than expected even though an index exists.
reasoning: Check whether index keys and predicates align.
Compare estimated and actual row counts and inspect buffers.
Account for result size, heap access, and write/storage trade-offs.
blocks.outcome: Make a targeted change only after plan evidence supports the hypothesis.

blocks.text: A partial index contains only rows satisfying its predicate, useful for stable subsets such as pending jobs. PostgreSQL can use it only when it can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX jobs_pending_created_idx ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.text: An expression index stores a computed value such as lower(email). The query expression must be compatible, and functions used in PostgreSQL index expressions must be immutable.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_lower_email_uq ON users (lower(email));

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Index type follows operators and data shape, not column labels.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 2
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: GIN can be costly to update; BRIN depends on physical correlation; partial/expression indexes require predicate/expression matching.

revisionSheet.text: B-tree supports common equality, range, and ordering patterns.
GIN is an inverted index for supported component-search operators.
GiST is operator-class-specific; BRIN summarizes physical block ranges.
Partial indexes contain only rows matching their predicate.
Expression indexes need compatible expressions and immutable functions.

questions.prompt: Which is the default starting point for scalar equality, range, and ordered scans?
questions.explanation: B-tree supports equality, range, and compatible ordering.

questions.prompt: A query uses JSONB containment with @>. Which is a common candidate?

options.text: GIN with compatible JSONB operator class

questions.explanation: GIN often supports JSONB containment, but operator class matters.

options.text: Huge table where values correlate with physical block order
Tiny table with random point lookups

questions.explanation: BRIN summarizes block ranges and can be tiny when physical correlation is strong.

options.text: It stores only rows satisfying its predicate
It stores all rows but compresses them
It always indexes the first column

questions.explanation: It is usable when the planner can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate.

questions.prompt: What does an index on lower(email) directly support?

options.text: Every query on every text column

questions.explanation: The query expression must align with the index expression.

questions.prompt: What is an important limitation of hash indexes?

options.text: Equality only; no ordered range traversal
They are the only index supporting equality

questions.explanation: Hash does not provide B-tree ordering/range behavior.

questions.prompt: What is GiST best understood as?

options.text: Generalized search-tree framework whose behavior depends on operator class
An inverted index only for JSONB

questions.explanation: GiST supports different searches through operator classes.

questions.prompt: A partial index has WHERE status='pending'. Which query is the direct fit?
questions.explanation: The query predicate implies the partial-index predicate.

options.text: BRIN for huge physically correlated data
Hash for ORDER BY timestamp and ranges

questions.explanation: B-tree, GIN, and BRIN serve different workloads; hash does not provide ordering.

questions.prompt: What should you check before adding a specialized index?
questions.explanation: Index selection depends on operators, data shape, and workload cost.

questions.prompt: BRIN stores a full ordered copy of every indexed value like a B-tree.
questions.explanation: BRIN stores block-range summaries and can require rechecks.

questions.prompt: An expression index on lower(email) automatically serves every predicate on email without lower().
questions.explanation: The query expression must be compatible with the index expression.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A PostgreSQL table has JSONB attributes and timestamps. Product needs JSONB containment and time-range reports. Recommend indexes.
strongAnswerPoints: Evaluate GIN for JSONB containment with a suitable opclass.
Evaluate B-tree for ordered time ranges; BRIN if huge and physically correlated.
Measure index size, write rate, rechecks, and plans.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would evaluate GIN for JSONB containment and B-tree for time-range/order queries. For a huge append-oriented table with strong time-to-heap-order correlation, BRIN may be smaller but lossy. Confirm operators/opclasses and benchmark using EXPLAIN ANALYZE and buffers.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A partial index on status='pending' is not used by a prepared query with a status parameter. What do you check?
strongAnswerPoints: Check if the planner can prove the query implies the index predicate.
Inspect generic/custom plan behavior where relevant.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The planner must prove the query predicate implies the partial-index predicate. A generic parameterized plan may not know the value is always pending. Inspect the actual plan and prepared-plan behavior before changing the design.
